\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself (how distributional features evolve across generation depths) remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using eight base (pretrained) models from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable for depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation; under this account, the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input content, while variance shows moderate drift.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves 3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding how distributional features evolve across generation depths is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When individual detection scores are repurposed as ordinal predictors, they span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and no single detector provides reliable depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; our focus on non-paraphrastic chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, is complementary.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving its shape: the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input, and each successive generation compresses the lower portion toward the model's preferred output distribution.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

\begin{abstract}
When LLM-generated text re-enters the web and seeds further generation, the resulting recursive chains exhibit progressively altered distributional properties.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding how distributional features evolve across generation depths is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When individual detection scores are repurposed as ordinal predictors, they span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and no single detector provides reliable depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; our focus on non-paraphrastic chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, is complementary.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving its shape: the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input, and each successive generation compresses the lower portion toward the model's preferred output distribution.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure this intrinsic mechanism; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The signal is prompt-type dependent (continuation chains show stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and despite the structured nature of depth-related distributional changes, depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling \cite{fineweb,dolma}.

    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation.

\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding how distributional features evolve across generation depths is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When individual detection scores are repurposed as ordinal predictors, they span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and no single detector provides reliable depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; our focus on non-paraphrastic chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, is complementary.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving its shape: the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input, and each successive generation compresses the lower portion toward the model's preferred output distribution.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure this intrinsic mechanism; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves 3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains), significantly outperforming individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
The signal is prompt-type dependent (continuation chains show stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and despite the structured nature of depth-related distributional changes, depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling \cite{fineweb,dolma}.

\end{enumerate}

\label{sec:results-classification}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), we also report a leak-free binary metric (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+): F1\,=\,0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700].
Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+ (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).
Depth signal persists at scale (Qwen3-8B: 0.692, Mistral-7B: 0.633), though larger generators show predictable degradation relative to the 0.694 average.

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold CV,\footnote{Cross-model chains use the original five-generator subset (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen); Llama and Mistral were added later for single-generator evaluation.} providing primary evidence of practical applicability: depth signal persists even when text passes through heterogeneous generators.
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields average binary F1\,=\,0.686 ($\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.8\,pp vs.\ LOGO), confirming transfer across architectural families under the strictest unseen-generator test.
Appendix~\ref{app:domain} further demonstrates that the signal generalizes across text domains (News, Academic, Code; binary F1 $>$ 0.73).

\paragraph{Length confound control.}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding how distributional features evolve across generation depths is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving its shape: the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input, and each successive generation compresses the lower portion toward the model's preferred output distribution.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure this intrinsic mechanism; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves 3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains), significantly outperforming individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
The signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across eight generators from five families and show that a 7-feature ensemble exploiting this structure significantly outperforms all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
    \item \textbf{Negative transfer to curation.} Despite the structured nature of depth-related distributional changes, depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling \cite{fineweb,dolma}.
\end{enumerate}
